# Visual Feedback {.transition}

## 

Speakers incorporate [visual cues]{.emph} in their L1 [@bernstein2004auditory] and L2 [@navarra2007hearing; @engwall2008can]

::: fragment

L2 classrooms typically avoid teaching pronunciation [@derwing2005second; @gilbert2014intonation] despite the benefits [@gordon2012pronunciation; @saito2015communicative]

:::

::: fragment

[Suprasegmentals]{.emph} have been taught with visual feedback [@chun2002discourse; @chun1998signal; @chun1989teaching]

:::

::: fragment

- ... but little has been done with [segmentals]{.emph} [@bliss2018computer]

::: 

##

[Indirect]{.emph} visual feedback includes e.g., spectrography

::: fragment

Spectrographic feedback resulted in improvements for vowels and consonants [@molholt1990spectrographic; @akahane1997second; @olson2014benefits; @niermann2016spectrographic]

:::

::: fragment

but...

:::

::: incremental

- steep learning curve
- does not provide an explanation of the user's error 
- or the articulatory cause of those errors [@rogerson2021computer; @wilson2014using]

:::

##

[Direct]{.emph} visual feedback provides information about articulators

::: fragment

Electromagnetic articulography (EMA) has produced gains in learner pronunciation of segments [@levitt2007augmented; @suemitsu2015real]

:::

::: fragment

... but EMA is prohibitively expensive for the teacher and uncomfortably intrusive for the learner

:::

##

[Ultrasound]{.emph} machines have become increasingly affordable, portable, and are non-invasive [@gick2005techniques]

::: incremental

History of use in...

- clinical setting [@dugan2023qualitative]
- teaching spoken language to the hard-of-hearing and deaf [@bernhardt2005ultrasound; @bernhardt2003speech]
- accent correction in L2 learners [@badin2010visual; @ouni2014tongue]

:::

::: fragment

Despite benefits, remains infrequently used in SLA research and the L2 classroom

:::

# Coronal Stop-Rhotic Clusters {.transition}

## Coronal Stops {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

stop_table <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("VOT lag","POA"),
  English = c("short/long", "alveolar"),
  Spanish = c("lead/short", "dental"),
  row.names = c("VOT", "POA")
) %>%
  flextable(.) %>%
  bold(part="header") %>%
  autofit()
  
stop_table
```

::: fragment 
Common to investigate L2 acquisition of VOT [@casillas2020longitudinal; @schuhmann2019development; @olson2022phonetic]

:::

::: fragment

Less common to investigate acquisition of place of articulation

:::

::: fragment

American English speakers can distinguish alveolar vs dental stops in Irish English with only slightly less accuracy than Irish English natives [@kelly2019perception]

:::

## Rhotics

[ɾ] is [phonemic]{.emph} in Spanish and [allophonic]{.emph} in English, but they're phonetically similar [@zue1979acoustic; @reetz2020phonetics]

::: fragment

Despite that, beginner L1 English L2 Spanish produce [ɾ] as [ɹ] [@weech2009second]

:::

::: fragment

Overall target-like production increases with proficiency [@face2006intervocalic] and experience [@weech2009second]

:::

::: fragment

But even 5th semester undergrads and graduate students in a Hispanic linguistics & literature program found that learners do not encode /ɾ r/ distinction in their lexicon [@daidone2014quierro]

:::

## Coronal Stop-Rhotic Clusters

/t d/ + rhotic onset clusters are phonotactically legal in both English & Spanish

::: fragment

Although the individual segments are relatively similar, the clusters are realized phonetically differently

:::

::: fragment

American English /tr dr/ are often pronounced as rhotacized post-alveolar affricates [@scobbie2006acquisition; @schwartz2023all; @cruttenden2014gimson; @carley2019american]

:::

::: fragment

Spanish /tɾ dɾ/ are often pronounced [tɾ dɾ]

:::

## Spanish Coronal Stop-Rhotic Clusters {.smaller}

L1 English L2 Spanish /tɾ dɾ/ production has been assessed with five measures [@gonzalez2023acquisition; @colantoni2006native; @morales2017development; @colantoni2018mixed]:

- stop VOT
- rhotic manner
- rhotic duration
- presence of epenthetic vowel
- duration of epenthetic vowel

::: fragment

Learners who receive spectrography training outperform control group on target-like production [@morales2017development]

:::

::: fragment

Target-like production does occur in advanced learners, but it's the exception [@colantoni2006native]

:::

##

L1 English L2 Spanish acquire coronal stop-rhotic cluster phonetics in specific order:

<br>

<center>
stop voicing > rhotic manner/duration >

presence/absence & duration of epenthetic vowel
</center>

::: fragment

Is this ordering sensitive to training?

:::

::: fragment

Rhotic manner and presence of epenthetic vowel seem dependent on POA of stop, but little explicit or direct investigation of stop placement in L1 English L2 Spanish learners

:::

::: footer

[@morales2017development; @colantoni2006native]

:::

# Perception-Production Link {.transition}

## 

::: fragment

Second Language Linguistic Perception [L2LP; @van2015learning] proposes perception precedes production [@casillas2020phonetic]

:::

::: fragment

So it seems unintuitive to train production before perception

:::

::: fragment

but...

:::

::: incremental

- we see that production can precede perception [@sheldon1982acquisition]
- some L2 models privilege the role of production [@swain2005output] 
- learners given articulatory instruction, instead of just "listen and repeat", perform better in production & perception [@catford1970auditory]

:::

# Research Questions {.transition}

1. First (production)

2. Second (production)

3. Third (perception)

4. Fourth (perception)

# Methods {.transition}

## Participants

- 20 L1 English L2 Spanish learners
  - 10 in experimental group
  - 10 in control group
- Proficiency level: A1
- Domestic immersion program

## Tasks

- Delayed shadowing (production)
- AXB discrimination (perception)
- AB identification (perception)

## Delayed Shadowing

- 30 target nonce words & 40 distractors
- target words: bisyllabic trVCV with penultimate stress
- each of five Spanish vowels represented first V six times
- Second syllable variably started with one of six stop consonants
- Final V always /a/
- Presented in random order & repeated three times each
- Recorded with ultrasound imaging

## AXB Discrimination & AB Identification

- Stimuli manipulated on two dimensions: place of articulation and voicing
- POA differences produced by native bilingual
- VOT differences manipulated in Praat

## Ultrasound Training {.smaller}

::: incremental 

- 30 to 45 mins
- Participants given ~10 mins of instructions during first training session
- Shown how to view midsaggital or coronal views
- Provided with .mp4 files of native Spanish speakers producing target clusters with time aligned audio and text 
- Provided with the following questions at each session [@olson2014benefits]:
  - Describe the visual difference between your production and pronunciation by a native Spanish speaker
  - Where is the Spanish speaker's tongue tip when they pronounce 't'?
  - Where is the Spanish speaker's tongue tip when they pronounce 'r'?

:::

## Procedure

Five sessions over five consecutive weeks

::: fragment

<center>At each session...</center>

:::

::: fragment

[Control]{.emph} group completed delayed shadowing -> AXB discrimination -> AB identification

:::

::: incremental

- [Experimental]{.emph} group completed delayed shadowing --> AXB discrimination --> AB identification

- At sessions 2, 3, and 4, they also completed 30-45 mins of [ultrasound training]{.emph}

:::

## Data Analysis

- Acoustic and perception judgements over the 5 sessions will be analyzed using generalized additive linear models

::: incremental

- "Magic moment" of ultrasound will be tongue tip contact for stop consonant
- Or looking for two points of contact (dental stop + alveolar tap)?
- Advice would be appreciated :-)

:::
